text: Niall Ferguson DOOM The Politics of Catastrophe
text_raw:
Niall Ferguson
DOOM
The Politics of Catastrophe

text: Contents List of Illustrations Introduction This is not a history of our perplexing postmodern plague, nor a general history of pandemics.
text_raw:
Contents
List of Illustrations
Introduction
This is not a history of our perplexing postmodern plague, nor a general history
of pandemics.

text: This is a general history of catastrophe—of all kinds of disasters, from the geological to the geopolitical, from the biological to the technological.
text_raw:
This is a general history of catastrophe—of all kinds of disasters,
from the geological to the geopolitical, from the biological to the technological.

text: For how else are we to see our disaster—or any disaster—in a proper perspective?
text_raw:
For how else are we to see our disaster—or any disaster—in a proper
perspective?

text: THE MEANING OF DEATH Though life expectancy has hugely improved in the modern era, death remains inevitable and is, in absolute terms, more common than ever.
text_raw:
THE MEANING OF DEATH
Though life expectancy has hugely improved in the modern era, death remains
inevitable and is, in absolute terms, more common than ever.

text: Yet we have become estranged from death.
text_raw:
Yet we have
become estranged from death.

text: Ultimately, not only are we as individuals doomed, but so is the human race itself.
text_raw:
Ultimately, not only are we as individuals
doomed, but so is the human race itself.

text: All the world religions and a number of secular ideologies have sought to make this eschaton seem more imminent (as well as immanent) than it really is.
text_raw:
All the world religions and a number of
secular ideologies have sought to make this eschaton seem more imminent (as
well as immanent) than it really is.

text: What we have to fear is a big disaster, not doomsday.
text_raw:
What we have to fear is a big disaster, not
doomsday.

text: Of the big disasters in human history, the biggest have been pandemics and wars.
text_raw:
Of the big disasters in human history, the biggest have been
pandemics and wars.

text: CYCLES AND TRAGEDIES Catastrophe is innately unpredictable because most disasters (from earthquakes to wars) are not normally distributed, but randomly or according to power laws.
text_raw:
CYCLES AND TRAGEDIES
Catastrophe is innately unpredictable because most disasters (from earthquakes
to wars) are not normally distributed, but randomly or according to power laws.

text: Cyclical theories of history cannot get around that.
text_raw: Cyclical theories of history cannot get around that.

text: Disasters are more like tragedies: those who try to predict them are unlikely to be heeded.
text_raw:
Disasters are more like
tragedies: those who try to predict them are unlikely to be heeded.

text: In addition to predicting more disasters than actually happen, Cassandras are up against a
text_raw:
In addition to
predicting more disasters than actually happen, Cassandras 
are up against a

text: bewildering array of cognitive biases.
text_raw: bewildering array of cognitive biases.

text: In the end, faced with uncertainty, most people just decide to ignore the possibility that they as individuals will be victims of catastrophe. “The bells of hell go ting-a-ling-a-ling for you but not for me,” a ditty sung by British soldiers in World War I, is humanity’s signature tune.
text_raw:
In the end, faced with uncertainty, most
people just decide to ignore the possibility that they as individuals will be
victims of catastrophe. “The bells of hell go ting-a-ling-a-ling for you but not for
me,” a ditty sung by British soldiers in World War I, is humanity’s signature
tune.

text: GRAY RHINOS, BLACK SWANS, AND DRAGON KINGS Disasters are often foreseen (gray rhinos), yet even some predicted disasters can appear completely unexpected when they strike (black swans).
text_raw:
GRAY RHINOS, BLACK SWANS, AND DRAGON KINGS
Disasters are often foreseen (gray rhinos), yet even some predicted disasters can
appear completely unexpected when they strike (black swans).

text: A few have consequences beyond excess mortality that set them apart (dragon kings).
text_raw:
A few have
consequences beyond excess mortality that set them apart (dragon kings).

text: Disasters are not either “natural” or “man-made.” Decisions to locate settlements near potential disaster zones—by a volcano, on a fault line, next to a river subject to severe flooding—are what make most natural disasters in some respects man-made.
text_raw:
Disasters are not either “natural” or “man-made.” Decisions to locate settlements
near potential disaster zones—by a volcano, on a fault line, next to a river
subject to severe flooding—are what make most natural disasters in some
respects man-made.

text: In terms of loss of life, more big disasters happen in Asia than elsewhere.
text_raw:
In terms of loss of life, more big disasters happen in Asia
than elsewhere.

text: The great American disaster has been, by Asian standards, not all that disastrous.
text_raw:
The great American disaster has been, by Asian standards, not
all that disastrous.

text: NETWORLD The decisive determinant of the scale of a disaster is whether or not there is contagion.
text_raw:
NETWORLD
The decisive determinant of the scale of a disaster is whether or not there is
contagion.

text: Social network structure is therefore as important as the innate properties of a pathogen or anything else (such as an idea) that can be virally spread.
text_raw:
Social network structure is therefore as important as the innate
properties of a pathogen or anything else (such as an idea) that can be virally
spread.

text: People worked out the efficacy of quarantines, social distancing, and other measures now referred to as “non-pharmaceutical interventions” long before they properly understood the true nature of the diseases they sought to counter, from smallpox to bubonic plague.
text_raw:
People worked out the efficacy of quarantines, social distancing, and
other measures now referred to as “non-pharmaceutical interventions” long
before they properly understood the true nature of the diseases they sought to
counter, from smallpox to bubonic plague.

text: The essence of such measures is to modify network structures to make it less of a small world.
text_raw:
The essence of such measures is to
modify network structures to make it less of a small world.

text: Such modifications can be spontaneous behavioral adaptations, but they usually need to be hierarchically mandated.
text_raw:
Such modifications
can be spontaneous behavioral adaptations, but they usually need to be
hierarchically mandated.

text: THE SCIENCE DELUSION The nineteenth century was a time of major advances, especially in bacteriology.
text_raw:
THE SCIENCE DELUSION
The nineteenth century was a time of major advances, especially in bacteriology.

text: But we should not succumb to a Whig interpretation of medical history.
text_raw: But we should not succumb to a Whig interpretation of medical history.

text: Empire forced the pace of research into infectious diseases, but it also forced the pace of
text_raw:
Empire
forced the pace of research into infectious diseases, but it also forced the pace of

text: the globalization of the world economy, creating new opportunities for diseases, not all of which submitted to vaccination or therapy.
text_raw:
the globalization of the world economy, creating new opportunities for diseases,
not all of which submitted to vaccination or therapy.

text: The 1918 influenza was a grim revelation of the limits of science.
text_raw:
The 1918 influenza was a
grim revelation of the limits of science.

text: Breakthroughs in our understanding of risks can be offset by increased network integration and fragility.
text_raw:
Breakthroughs in our understanding of
risks can be offset by increased network integration and fragility.

text: THE PSYCHOLOGY OF POLITICAL INCOMPETENCE We tend to attribute too much of the responsibility for political disasters, as well as military ones, to incompetent leaders.
text_raw:
THE PSYCHOLOGY OF POLITICAL INCOMPETENCE
We tend to attribute too much of the responsibility for political disasters, as well
as military ones, to incompetent leaders.

text: It was a pleasing argument of the Indian economist Amartya Sen that famines were caused by unaccountable governments and avoidable market failures, not food shortages per se, and that democracy was the best cure for famines.
text_raw:
It was a pleasing argument of the Indian
economist Amartya Sen that famines were caused by unaccountable
governments and avoidable market failures, not food shortages per se, and that
democracy was the best cure for famines.

text: That theory may well explain some of the worst famines in the century and a half from the 1840s to the 1990s.
text_raw:
That theory may well explain some of
the worst famines in the century and a half from the 1840s to the 1990s.

text: But why should Sen’s law apply only to famines?
text_raw:
But why
should Sen’s law apply only to famines?

text: Why not to the most man-made of disasters, wars?
text_raw:
Why not to the most man-made of
disasters, wars?

text: It is a paradox that the transition from empires to more or less democratic nation-states was attended by so much death and destruction.
text_raw:
It is a paradox that the transition from empires to more or less
democratic nation-states was attended by so much death and destruction.

text: FROM THE BOOGIE WOOGIE FLU TO EBOLA IN TOWN In 1957, the rational response to a new and deadly strain of flu seemed to be a combination of pursuing natural herd immunity and selective vaccination.
text_raw:
FROM THE BOOGIE WOOGIE FLU TO EBOLA IN TOWN
In 1957, the rational response to a new and deadly strain of flu seemed to be a
combination of pursuing natural herd immunity and selective vaccination.

text: There were no lockdowns and no school closures, despite the fact that the Asian flu in 1957 was about as dangerous as COVID-19 in 2020.
text_raw:
There
were no lockdowns and no school closures, despite the fact that the Asian flu in
1957 was about as dangerous as COVID-19 in 2020.

text: The success of Eisenhower’s response reflected not only the nimbleness of the federal government of those days but also the Cold War context of much-improved international cooperation on issues of public health.
text_raw:
The success of
Eisenhower’s response reflected not only the nimbleness of the federal
government of those days but also the Cold War context of much-improved
international cooperation on issues of public health.

text: Yet the successes of the 1950s, ’60s, and ’70s were deceptive.
text_raw:
Yet the successes of the
1950s, ’60s, and ’70s were deceptive.

text: HIV/AIDS revealed the weaknesses of both national and international agencies.
text_raw:
HIV/AIDS revealed the weaknesses of
both national and international agencies.

text: So, in their different ways, did SARS, MERS, and Ebola.
text_raw:
So, in their different ways, did SARS,
MERS, and Ebola.

text: THE FRACTAL GEOMETRY OF DISASTER Accidents will happen, from the Titanic to Challenger to Chernobyl.
text_raw:
THE FRACTAL GEOMETRY OF DISASTER
Accidents will happen, from the 
Titanic
 to 
Challenger
 to Chernobyl.

text: Small disasters are like microcosms of big ones, but because they are less complex, we can understand them more easily.
text_raw:
Small
disasters are like microcosms of big ones, but because they are less complex, we
can understand them more easily.

text: The common feature of all disasters, whether sinking ships or exploding nuclear reactors, is the combination of operator error
text_raw:
The common feature of all disasters, whether
sinking ships or exploding nuclear reactors, is the combination of operator error

text: and managerial error.
text_raw: and managerial error.

text: Often the point of failure in a disaster is not at the top (the “blunt end”) or at the point of contact (the “sharp end”) but within middle management—a favorite theme of the physicist Richard Feynman and an insight with general applicability.
text_raw:
Often the point of failure in a disaster is not at the top (the
“blunt end”) or at the point of contact (the “sharp end”) but within middle
management—a favorite theme of the physicist Richard Feynman and an insight
with general applicability.

text: THE PLAGUES Like so many past pandemics, COVID-19 originated in China.
text_raw:
THE PLAGUES
Like so many past pandemics, COVID-19 originated in China.

text: But the varied impact of the disease on the rest of the world’s countries confounded expectations.
text_raw:
But the varied
impact of the disease on the rest of the world’s countries confounded
expectations.

text: Far from being well prepared for a pandemic, the United States and the United Kingdom fared badly.
text_raw:
Far from being well prepared for a pandemic, the United States and
the United Kingdom fared badly.

text: It was countries such as Taiwan and South Korea that had learned the right lessons from SARS and MERS.
text_raw:
It was countries such as Taiwan and South
Korea that had learned the right lessons from SARS and MERS.

text: It was tempting to blame Anglo-American travails on the incompetence of populist leaders.
text_raw:
It was tempting
to blame Anglo-American travails on the incompetence of populist leaders.

text: However, something more profound had gone wrong.
text_raw: However, something more profound had gone wrong.

text: The public health bureaucracy in each case had failed.
text_raw:
The public health
bureaucracy in each case had failed.

text: And the role of the internet platforms in disseminating fake news about COVID-19 led to poor and sometimes downright harmful adaptations in public behavior.
text_raw:
And the role of the internet platforms in
disseminating fake news about COVID-19 led to poor and sometimes downright
harmful adaptations in public behavior.

text: THE ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES OF THE PLAGUE The shift from complacency to panic in mid-March 2020 led to economically crushing lockdowns in many countries.
text_raw:
THE ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES OF THE PLAGUE
The shift from complacency to panic in mid-March 2020 led to economically
crushing lockdowns in many countries.

text: Were they the right solutions to the problem posed by COVID-19?
text_raw:
Were they the right solutions to the
problem posed by COVID-19?

text: The answer is probably not, but that did not make it smart for the United States to attempt a return to normality that summer (the dumb reopening) without adequate testing and tracing.
text_raw:
The answer is probably not, but that did not make
it smart for the United States to attempt a return to normality that summer (the
dumb reopening) without adequate testing and tracing.

text: The predictable result was a second, smaller wave and a “tortoise-shaped” recovery.
text_raw:
The predictable result
was a second, smaller wave and a “tortoise-shaped” recovery.

text: Less predictable was the near-revolutionary political eruption over the issue of racism, which bore striking resemblances to mass movements precipitated by previous pandemics.
text_raw:
Less predictable
was the near-revolutionary political eruption over the issue of racism, which
bore striking resemblances to mass movements precipitated by previous
pandemics.

text: THE THREE-BODY PROBLEM The COVID-19 crisis is widely regarded as dooming the United States to decline relative to China.
text_raw:
THE THREE-BODY PROBLEM
The COVID-19 crisis is widely regarded as dooming the United States to decline
relative to China.

text: This is probably wrong.
text_raw: This is probably wrong.

text: The empires of our time—the United States, China, and the European Union—all made a mess of the pandemic in their different ways.
text_raw:
The empires of our time—the United
States, China, and the European Union—all made a mess of the pandemic in
their different ways.

text: But it is hard to see why the countries that handled it well
text_raw: But it is hard to see why the countries that handled it well

text: would be eager to join Xi Jinping’s imperial panopticon.
text_raw: would be eager to join Xi Jinping’s imperial panopticon.

text: In a number of respects, the crisis has shown the persistence of American power: in financial terms, in the race for a vaccine, and in the technological competition.
text_raw:
In a number of
respects, the crisis has shown the persistence of American power: in financial
terms, in the race for a vaccine, and in the technological competition.

text: Rumors of American doom are once again exaggerated.
text_raw:
Rumors of
American doom are once again exaggerated.

text: Perhaps because of this exaggeration, the risk of not just cold but hot war is rising.
text_raw:
Perhaps because of this
exaggeration, the risk of not just cold but hot war is rising.

text: Conclusion FUTURE SHOCKS We have no way of knowing what the next disaster will be.
text_raw:
Conclusion
FUTURE SHOCKS
We have no way of knowing what the next disaster will be.

text: Our modest goal should be to make our societies and political systems more resilient—and ideally antifragile—than they currently are.
text_raw:
Our modest goal
should be to make our societies and political systems more resilient—and ideally
antifragile—than they currently are.

text: That requires a better understanding of network structure and of bureaucratic dysfunction than we currently possess.
text_raw:
That requires a better understanding of
network structure and of bureaucratic dysfunction than we currently possess.

text: Those who would acquiesce in a new totalitarianism of ubiquitous surveillance in the name of public safety have failed to appreciate that some of the worst disasters described in this book were caused by totalitarian regimes.
text_raw:
Those who would acquiesce in a new totalitarianism of ubiquitous surveillance
in the name of public safety have failed to appreciate that some of the worst
disasters described in this book were caused by totalitarian regimes.

text: 27 A remarkable paper by the young Korean scholar Jaeweon Shin and coauthors proposes a refinement of Turchin’s model that introduces information technology as a variable. “Sociopolitical development,” they write, “is dominated first by growth in polity scale, then by improvements in information processing and economic systems, and then by further increases in scale.” There may, they suggest, be a “Scale Threshold for societies, beyond which growth in information processing becomes paramount, and an Information Threshold, which once crossed facilitates additional growth in scale.” 28 Looking especially at the failure of New World societies (with the possible exception of the one in Cuzco) to develop systems of written record, they ask, “Could some of the frequent collapses seen in societies be due to a polity’s never developing sufficient information-processing capacities, so that it stumbles or even collapses through poor performance due to lack of external connectivity, internal coherence, or inability to compete with polities whose superior information-processing abilities have enabled more growth in size?” 29 Yet, as Turchin and Nefedov acknowledge, any cyclical process must itself be subject to distinctly noncyclical forces: extreme climate fluctuations, pandemics, and technological discontinuities, as well as major conflicts, which, as we have seen, have an almost random incidence in terms of both timing and scale.

The governor of Bengal, Sir John Herbert, was dying of cancer in Government
House; the outgoing viceroy, the Marquess of Linlithgow, acquiesced as the
other provincial governments kept their food to themselves, while price-fixing
measures simply encouraged wholesalers to hoard.

text: One of the villains of the piece was the minister for civil supplies, an Oxford graduate named Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy, who was suspected by Linlithgow’s successor of having “siphoned money from every project that was undertaken to ease the famine, and awarded to his associates contracts for warehousing, the sale of grain to governments, and transportation.” 46 (Hoary old arguments that the indigenous elites would treat the Indian masses worse than the British began to ring true.) As The Statesman put it on September 23, “This sickening catastrophe is man made”—the result of a “shameful lack of planning capacity and foresight by India’s own civil Governments, Central and Provincial.” 47 What changed the situation was in fact Churchill’s decision to appoint Wavell as viceroy.

text: revealing essay published last April, the Chinese political theorist Jiang Shigong, a professor at Peking University Law School, spelled out the corollary of American decline. “The history of humanity is surely the history of competition for imperial hegemony,” Jiang wrote, “which has gradually propelled the form of empires from their original local nature toward the current tendency toward global empires, and finally toward a single world empire.” The globalization of our time, according to Jiang, is the “‘single world empire’ 1.0, the model of world empire established by England and the United States.” But that Anglo- American empire is “unravelling” internally, because of “three great unsolvable problems: the ever-increasing inequality created by the liberal economy … ineffective governance caused by political liberalism, and decadence and nihilism created by cultural liberalism.” Moreover, the Western Empire is under external attack from “Russian resistance and Chinese competition.” This is not a bid to create an alternative Eurasian empire, but “a struggle to become the heart of the world empire.” 134 If you doubt that China is seeking to take over empire 1.0 and turn it into empire 2.0, based on China’s illiberal civilization, then you are not paying attention to all the ways this strategy is being executed.
